question_or_symptom: The two-phase journal used atomic rename but did not fully specify durability for its namespace or the Git objects and refs that it names.
observation: Without fsync of the parent that first publishes txn/, a crash can lose the active journal directory. During retirement, persisting the source-directory deletion before the destination-directory addition can lose the only durable name. Separately, a durable journal can still point at a recently created loose commit or tree that Git has not fsynced under its default configuration.
conclusion: Atomic rename alone is not a durable cross-repository transaction protocol; journal namespaces, referenced Git object closure, refs, indexes, directory ordering, and possible post-crash states are all part of the state machine.
decision: Persist newly created journal directories through their parent, fsync the retirement destination before the source, and recover dual active/retired names only when their bytes are identical. Before publishing journal transitions, write child commits, prepared root trees, and the coordinator commit to non-thin packs, fsync pack indexes and refs, and reject detached or linked-worktree layouts whose ref ownership is ambiguous. Conflicting duplicate journals remain a hard failure.
invalidated_assumptions: An atomic os.replace call makes a cross-directory journal move crash-durable without ordered directory fsyncs and duplicate recovery.
A successfully created Git commit or tree is necessarily durable before a separately fsynced transaction journal references it.
